strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: detecting changes in social bias after continued masked-language-model training. Comparing a retrained model with its pretrained base is a sensible diagnostic approach.

The empirical study covers four MLMs, two established benchmarks, several baseline measures, and detailed results by bias category. Explicit equations, checkpoint identifiers, dataset counts, and token-level examples help readers inspect the intended methodology.

Retraining in both stereotype directions provides a useful sensitivity check. CRR, ΔP, and ΔPA recover the expected direction across all 72 model/category/retraining-condition cases, supporting further investigation of prediction-quality measures.
weaknesses: The central claim of more accurate bias measurement is insufficiently validated. CPS supplies both retraining sentences and the reported bias evaluation; the stated 80/20 training/validation split does not establish an independent test. Expected labels are assigned from the retraining condition, so success can reflect fitting the selected sentences. Pair-disjoint evaluation and neutral or balanced retraining controls are needed to distinguish social-bias changes from general prediction improvements. The evidence supports a sensitivity claim, but the stronger accuracy and baseline 'underestimation' claims remain unresolved.

Human-annotation validation is weak. Figures 4–5 show best AUROCs of 0.572 versus AUL's 0.566 for RoBERTa, and 0.571 versus 0.569 for BERT. These small differences lack confidence intervals or significance tests, with only 58 negative pairs versus 1,450 positive pairs. Moreover, annotations identify biased sentence content rather than independently establish a particular model's biased behavior. The statement about selecting thresholds to maximize AUROC also needs clarification, since AUROC summarizes performance across thresholds.

The bias-change score and its statistical validation need correction. Equation 10 returns BSRT = 0 for identical models, although scores below 50 are interpreted as decreased bias; ties and unchanged models require explicit neutral treatment. Appendix P's McNemar test concerns changes in binary within-model preference signs, whereas BSRT concerns changes in continuous pairwise margins. Its significance markers therefore do not establish that BSRT differs from 50 or that one measure is more accurate. Uncertainty across retraining runs is also unreported.

The added value of the proposed components is not isolated. Previously proposed, unweighted CRR already achieves the same perfect directional classification as ΔPA, while CRRA makes one error. CRRA changes the rank transformation from 1−1/r to 1+log(r) while introducing attention, confounding two modifications. Separate transformation and attention ablations, together with an all-token pseudo-log-likelihood baseline, would clarify what produces the gains.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript. The announced package has no identifiable name or repository link, and learning rate, optimizer, batch size, random seeds, and precise attention aggregation are unspecified. Baseline definitions also conflict with the prose: Equations 11–12 sum over all sentence tokens, although CSPS and SSS are described as scoring unmodified and modified tokens respectively. These ambiguities affect the central comparisons.

Numerical reporting requires an audit. Table 3 reports a CSPS error rate of 0.028 for BERT retrained on stereotypical sentences, although Table 16 shows one error among nine categories, implying 0.111. Its BERT anti-stereotypical AULA entry also fails to reflect the four wrong-direction categories in Table 16. These discrepancies, alongside the unresolved validation and reproducibility issues, prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version.
